lesson.title: The Transition State: A Molecule Caught Mid-Transformation
lesson.summary: The transition state is the fleeting, highest-energy arrangement of atoms that a reacting molecule passes through as old bonds break and new ones form, and it is this exact arrangement that enzymes are specialized to stabilize.
lesson.body:
The transition state is the specific, unstable configuration of atoms that sits at the very peak of the activation energy barrier, midway between reactants and products. In this configuration, the bonds present in the reactant are partially broken, and the bonds that will define the product are partially formed, but neither set of bonds is complete. It is not a stable intermediate that can be isolated, bottled, or observed sitting around, it is closer to a molecular passing point than a molecular species. Estimates for how long a typical transition state persists are on the order of the time it takes a single bond to vibrate, an extraordinarily short span, which is part of why transition states cannot be captured directly with ordinary chemical techniques.

The transition state occupies the highest point on a reaction's energy diagram precisely because partially broken and partially formed bonds are less stable, and therefore higher in energy, than either fully intact reactant bonds or fully formed product bonds. The height of that peak above the reactants is what the previous chapter called the activation energy. Every reacting molecule has to pass through some version of this unstable peak on its way from reactant to product, regardless of whether the overall reaction is endergonic or exergonic.

This is where enzymes do most of their real work. A widely accepted explanation for enzyme catalysis, first proposed by the chemist Linus Pauling, holds that an enzyme's active site is shaped to bind the transition state of its reaction more tightly than it binds either the substrate or the product. Because the enzyme active site stabilizes this fleeting, high energy arrangement, it effectively lowers the energy of the peak relative to the reactants, which is the same thing as lowering the activation energy. This idea builds directly on the concept of the enzyme substrate complex: substrate binding is only the entry point, and the true catalytic payoff comes from how the enzyme handles the substrate as it is pushed toward, and briefly held at, the transition state.

A concrete illustration comes from serine proteases such as chymotrypsin, which cleave peptide bonds through a mechanism that passes through a tetrahedral transition state, a fleeting arrangement in which the carbon atom of the peptide bond briefly holds four different groups arranged around it rather than the flat, three group arrangement typical of a stable peptide bond. Many serine proteases have a small pocket near the active site, called an oxyanion hole, formed by backbone amide groups that hydrogen bond to and stabilize the negatively charged oxygen that develops on the substrate specifically during this tetrahedral transition state, illustrating transition state stabilization in a very literal, structural way.

The transition state concept also has practical importance beyond basic enzymology. Because enzymes bind the transition state of their reaction especially tightly, chemists designing drugs sometimes create transition state analogs, stable molecules built to mimic the shape and charge distribution of a reaction's transition state without actually reacting. Such molecules can bind an enzyme's active site with very high affinity and effectively shut the enzyme down, a strategy that has informed the design of certain enzyme inhibitors. Understanding the transition state, then, is not just an abstract detail of the energy diagram, it is central to explaining both how natural catalysis works and how it can be deliberately blocked.
